# Results — Study 840 (Clustered Standard Errors): the naive *t* lies, Fama-MacBeth doesn't

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). This is a **research-method demo**:
a pure Monte-Carlo simulation with no market data, no network, and no cache. We build a
mean-zero (null) panel carrying a **common time effect** — a shock shared by every firm in a
period (the Petersen 2009 cross-sectional dependence) — then compare the rejection rate of the
**naive i.i.d. OLS *t*** and one-way **firm** clustering against **time** clustering and
**Fama-MacBeth**. The synthetic core is deterministic under the config seed. Frozen as-of
**2026-06-30** (the simulation stamp — this is a sim study, so the "tape" is the config, not a
calendar month). Match the fingerprints to confirm you hold the same simulation.*

## The headline — a common time effect, β = 0 (so every rejection is a false positive)

On a panel we *built* to have a **zero** slope but a shared per-period shock in both the
regressor and the residual (each with intra-period correlation 0.5, N = 50 firms, T = 50
periods). The pooled slope is unbiased (Monte-Carlo mean **−0.00302 ≈ 0**); the damage is
**entirely in the standard error**. The Monte-Carlo SD of the pooled slope — the *truth* — is
**0.07525**; a calibrated SE should equal it (ratio ≈ 1):

| estimator | false-positive rate | Wilson95 | mean SE | SE / true SD | naive-*t* SD |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Nominal (α) | **5.00%** | — | — | 1.00 | 1.00 |
| **NAIVE i.i.d. OLS** | **60.4%** | [58.2%, 62.5%] | 0.01999 | **0.266** | **3.785** |
| **one-way firm clustering** | **66.2%** | [64.0%, 68.2%] | 0.01735 | **0.230** | 4.445 |
| **one-way time clustering** | **7.4%** | [6.3%, 8.6%] | 0.07024 | 0.933 | 1.116 |
| **Fama-MacBeth** | **5.3%** | [4.4%, 6.4%] | 0.02045 | **1.003** | 1.013 |

The naive OLS *t* rejects a **true** null **60% of the time** — twelve times the 5% it
advertises — because it treats 2,500 cross-sectionally-correlated observations as if they were
independent: its SE is only **27%** of the estimate's true sampling variability. The closed-form
Moulton (1986) inflation factor is **√(1 + (N−1)·ρ_x·ρ_e) = √13.25 = 3.640**, and the simulated
naive-*t* SD (3.785) lands right on it. **Clustering on the wrong dimension makes it worse, not
better:** one-way **firm** clustering (66.2%) fails because the dependence here is *across firms
within a period*, not within a firm over time — there is nothing for it to catch. **Time
clustering** (7.4%, a small documented few-cluster over-rejection with only T = 50 clusters) and
**Fama-MacBeth** (5.3%, bang on nominal, SE ratio 1.003) restore calibration.

## The control — switch the common time factor OFF and the pitfall vanishes

Set ρ_x = ρ_e = 0: no shared per-period shock, so the panel is i.i.d. across both dimensions.
Same generator, same estimators, only the cross-sectional dependence removed:

| estimator | false-positive rate |
|---|--:|
| NAIVE i.i.d. OLS | **4.95%** (back at nominal) |
| one-way firm clustering | 5.40% |
| one-way time clustering | 4.75% |
| Fama-MacBeth | 5.30% |

Naive-*t* SD **0.991** (SE ratio **1.009**) — no inflation. All four estimators are calibrated
when there is no dependence; the naive *t* is only dangerous *because of* the common time
factor. (Row-shuffling an already-drawn panel is **not** a valid placebo — the pooled slope and
its naive SE are invariant to relabelling the observations. The cause has to be removed at
generation, which is what ρ = 0 does.)

## Inflation vs the amount of cross-sectional dependence

**Residual intra-period correlation ρ_e** (ρ_x = 0.5, N = 50):

| ρ_e | naive OLS FP | firm FP | time FP | FM FP | naive-*t* SD | √(1+(N−1)ρ_xρ_e) |
|---:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 0.0 | 4.6% | 5.1% | 5.7% | 5.3% | 0.997 | 1.000 |
| 0.2 | 43.5% | 46.4% | 7.4% | 5.3% | 2.525 | 2.429 |
| 0.4 | 55.9% | 60.5% | 7.3% | 5.3% | 3.415 | 3.286 |
| 0.6 | 63.9% | 69.5% | 7.5% | 5.3% | 4.125 | 3.962 |
| 0.8 | 67.9% | 75.0% | 8.1% | 5.3% | 4.744 | 4.539 |

**Cross-section size N** (ρ_x = ρ_e = 0.5):

| N | naive OLS FP | firm FP | time FP | FM FP | naive-*t* SD | √(1+(N−1)ρ_xρ_e) |
|---:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 2 | 8.5% | 39.8% | 6.8% | 2.5% | 1.140 | 1.118 |
| 5 | 15.8% | 29.1% | 5.9% | 5.9% | 1.376 | 1.414 |
| 10 | 27.9% | 38.7% | 7.3% | 6.0% | 1.847 | 1.803 |
| 25 | 46.4% | 54.2% | 7.8% | 4.5% | 2.675 | 2.646 |
| 50 | 60.4% | 66.1% | 7.3% | 5.3% | 3.785 | 3.640 |
| 100 | 69.6% | 73.3% | 6.5% | 5.1% | 5.100 | 5.074 |

The empirical naive-*t* SD tracks the closed-form Moulton factor to within finite-sample error
across the board (the small consistent excess over theory shrinks as T grows). The naive
false-positive rate climbs monotonically with both dials, while Fama-MacBeth stays pinned at ~5%
throughout. Note the small-N firm row (N = 2 → 39.8%): one-way clustering with **very few
clusters** is itself badly mis-sized — clustering is not a free lunch.

## The positive control — the machinery still fires on a real effect

Plant a genuine slope `beta = 0.06` into the panel (same common time effect):

| Quantity | Value |
|---|--:|
| Fama-MacBeth rejection rate (power) | **84.0%** |
| Mean Fama-MacBeth *t* | **+2.99** |
| Share of FM *t* > 0 (correct sign) | **99.7%** |
| Mean FM slope (recovers β = 0.06) | **+0.0604** |

Fama-MacBeth is not merely conservative — hand it a real slope and it rejects the null 84% of
the time, recovers the planted magnitude (0.0604 vs 0.06), and gets the sign right 99.7% of the
time. The correction removes the *false* positives without killing the *true* ones.

## The timer — there is, by construction, nothing to trade

Costing one null panel as a notional dollar-neutral long-short on the noise predictor `x`
(full rebalance each period at 5 bps/side + 50 bps/yr borrow on the short leg, nominal 1%
return scale): gross **−3.14 bps/period** (indistinguishable from zero), net **−10.17
bps/period**, or **−25.6%** annualised. A null minus costs is a guaranteed loser — a Mirage by
construction.

## Verdict

- **Signal — NONE.** The panel is a *constructed null*: its true slope is zero, so there is
  nothing real to find. Fama-MacBeth correctly declines to reject (5.3% ≈ nominal). No robust
  |*t*| ≥ 2 on any honest tape exists here because the honest tape is empty by design; the only
  thing that "rejects" is a broken (or wrongly-clustered) standard error.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** Nothing to harvest. The apparent significance the naive *t*
  manufactures is a standard-error artefact, not a return; costed, the null loses **−25.6%/yr**.
- **Does cross-sectional dependence break naive inference? — CONFIRMED.** On a mean-zero panel
  with a common time effect the naive OLS false-positive rate is **60%** (12× nominal), the
  naive *t* is inflated by the closed-form Moulton factor **√13.25 ≈ 3.64×**, the inflation
  tracks √(1+(N−1)ρ_xρ_e) to within finite-sample error across ρ_e and N, **one-way firm
  clustering makes it worse (66%)** because it clusters on the wrong dimension, the
  no-dependence control is perfectly calibrated, and **Fama-MacBeth** restores nominal error
  (5.3%) while still detecting a planted effect at 84% power. The pitfall is real, measurable,
  and correctable — cluster on the dimension of the dependence (or use Fama-MacBeth / two-way
  clustering), never trust a naive *t* on a panel with a common time shock.
